transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, to be honest, Dr. ____, I'm really only here because my husband... well, my husband and the people down at the warehouse, they all keep acting like I'm crazy. Like I'm just making things up or losing my mind or something. But I'm not. I know exactly what's going on and I'm not stupid. 

I work freight, you know, moving materials and loading trucks all day, and there's this supervisor spot that opened up recently. I've been working really hard for it. But ever since it did, it's like... it's like suddenly everyone on the floor is clocking my every single move. I can feel them watching me from the upper racks, keeping tabs on where I take the pallet jack, how long I'm in the loading bay, who I talk to... all of it. 

And the worst part, the thing that really proves they're out to get me, is the pallet counts. I know how many pallets I wrap and move in a shift. I count them myself. But they’ve been sneaking into the system and changing my pallet counts at the end of the day just to make my numbers look bad. They’re doing it on purpose to keep me from getting that supervisor spot. And when I try to explain all this to my husband, how they're sabotaging my logs and watching me, he just looks at me like I'm the one who's not making sense and tells me I need to see a doctor. But I know what I see. I know they're messing with my counts, no matter what anyone says.
Have you ever had a period of several days or more when you felt unusually energized or elated and needed much less sleep than usual?

Well, see, energized is... it's a funny word for it. Because, yeah, sure, I have these stretches, maybe a week or so at a time, where I just feel completely fired up. Like, my blood is humming, you know? I'll be down at the warehouse, pulling double the pallets anyone else is pulling, moving so fast it's like I'm gliding across the concrete, and I don't even need to sleep. I'll get maybe two, three hours a night, tops, and I wake up feeling like a million bucks. Like nobody in the whole world can slow me down, let alone those guys on the floor trying to mess with my numbers. I feel unstoppable. 

But... elated? Happy? I don't know about that. Because when I'm like that, when my engine is just revving and revving, I get so... so on edge. Especially at home. Like, I'll walk in the door after a twelve-hour shift, completely wired, ready to clean the whole house or reorganize the garage, and my husband will just ask me one tiny, stupid little question. Like, "Did you pick up the kids' permission slips?" or "What time are you working tomorrow?" And I just... I snap. I completely bite his head off. I start yelling because it feels like he's trying to trap me, you know? Like he's trying to control my time or box me in when I have all this energy and all these things I need to get done. He looks at me like I'm a monster, but he just doesn't get how fast my brain is moving. He's moving in slow motion and dragging me down with him. So, yeah, energized, definitely. But it's not a fun kind of energy. It's like a live wire just whipping around, and if he gets too close with his questions, he's gonna get shocked.
Have you ever had times when the suspiciousness or feeling that people were watching or sabotaging you continued even when your mood and energy were back to normal?

Well, yeah, actually. Because that's the thing, Dr. ____, that's what I keep trying to tell my husband, but he just doesn't listen. It's not just when I'm wired up and running on two hours of sleep. Even when things calm down, you know? Like, there was this stretch a little while back, maybe a few weeks, where I was actually sleeping okay. I mean, closer to normal, maybe six or seven hours, and I wasn't moving like a freight train all over the warehouse. I was just doing my job, regular pace, not yelling at my husband when I got home, just... quieter, I guess you could say. 

But even then, even when my energy was totally fine and I wasn't feeling all revved up, I still knew they were messing with me. I mean, the proof was right there in the system! I would check the logs, and my pallet counts were still wrong. They were still changing them. And it's not just a feeling, because I can hear it, too. Like, even when I was feeling totally level, I'd still hear this voice, clear as day, just telling me to double-check my wraps, check the logs, check the loading dock, because they were coming for my numbers. The voice doesn't stop just because I'm getting a full night's sleep, you know? It's always there, reminding me to watch my back, because those guys on the floor don't take a break from trying to sabotage me just because I'm having a calm week. So, yeah, it definitely continues. The mood stuff, the energy, that comes and goes, but the sabotaging? That's constant. They never stop.
Have you ever had a period when you felt so unusually elevated or irritable that you were talking much more than usual and other people had trouble interrupting you?

Well, I mean, I don't really know about talking more than usual, because I've always been someone who likes to explain things properly, you know? Like, if you don't lay out all the details, people just don't get the full picture. Especially at the warehouse, you have to be clear. If you just say "move the pallet," they might move it to the wrong bay, or they might not wrap it right, and then who gets blamed? Me, probably, since they're already trying to ruin my numbers. So I've always been thorough. 

But as for people having trouble interrupting me... I don't really think so? I mean, my husband says sometimes I don't let him get a word in edgewise, especially when I'm in one of those revved-up moods I was telling you about, but honestly, that's just because he takes so incredibly long to get to the point. He'll start a sentence, and then he'll just pause, and look at the ceiling, and I'm standing there with my brain moving a million miles a minute, thinking about the kids' lunches, and the laundry, and how I need to get to work early to check the logs before the shift supervisor gets there. So, yeah, maybe I talk over him a little bit, or I just keep talking because if I stop, I'll lose my train of thought, and it's important stuff I'm trying to get across. But I wouldn't say I'm talking *too* much, just... efficiently, I guess? And if people can't keep up or feel like they can't interrupt, maybe they just need to listen faster, you know? Because I don't really notice myself being like a chatterbox or anything, just trying to make sure everything gets said that needs to be said before they can twist my words around.
Have you ever heard voices or had other psychotic symptoms for at least two weeks when you were not having any manic or depressive symptoms?

Well, like I was saying before, yes. Absolutely. Because it’s not just when my engine is revving, you know? Like I said, there was that stretch—maybe a month ago, or a little less, I don't know, time gets a little blurry when you work the shifts I do—but there were a solid few weeks where I was actually okay. Mood-wise, I mean. I wasn't snapping at my husband about the permission slips, I wasn't feeling like I could run a marathon after a twelve-hour shift, and I wasn't down in the dumps either. I was just... normal. I was sleeping my six or seven hours, waking up, having my coffee, going to the warehouse, and doing my job. Just regular. 

But even then, for those whole few weeks, the voice was still there. It didn't take a vacation just because I was getting some decent sleep. I'd be standing there, totally calm, wrapping a pallet, and I'd hear it just as clear as you and me talking right now. It would say, "Check the logs, they're messing with your numbers." Or "Look at the loading dock, they're moving your freight." And I knew it was true, because I'd go check the system, and the counts were still wrong. Even when I wasn't wired, even when I was totally level and not having any of those crazy energy spikes or feeling irritable, I still knew they were sabotaging me, and I still heard that voice warning me about it every single day for weeks. It’s like they know I’m paying attention, so they have to keep trying to ruin me, and the voice is just trying to keep me one step ahead, whether I'm feeling energized or just totally regular. So, yes, it definitely happens even when my mood is completely fine.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing voices or feeling paranoid, but you did not have any manic or depressive symptoms at the same time?

Well, I mean, I feel like I've been trying to say this, Dr. ____, but yes. Yes, definitely. Like I was just explaining about that stretch—it was maybe a month ago, or around then. It was a solid block of time, definitely more than two weeks, where I was just... quiet, you know? Like, my body wasn't humming, my brain wasn't buzzing. I was actually sleeping closer to normal, getting my six, maybe seven hours, which is huge for me, because normally I'm lucky if I get three before I'm up pacing the kitchen and writing down all the things I need to double-check at the warehouse. 

But during this time, I wasn't racing around like a maniac, I wasn't snapping at my husband or the kids, I wasn't feeling like I could take on the world or like I was dragging a boulder behind me. I was just going to work, doing my job, coming home, making dinner... just normal, regular life. But the thing is, even during those quieter weeks, the paranoia—well, I don't even like calling it paranoia because it's real, but the feeling that they were after me—it didn't stop. And the voice didn't stop either. I'd be standing there, totally calm, not hyped up at all, and I'd still hear it telling me to check the logs, check the wraps, check the loading dock. And I still completely believed—because I saw it in the system—that they were changing my pallet counts to make me look bad. So, yeah, the mood stuff was completely gone for those weeks, but the voice and the sabotage? They were still right there with me every single day.
During those times when you were hearing the voice, was it ever accompanied by a depressed mood?

Well, I mean... no, not really. Because, like I said, those weeks where I was hearing the voice but wasn't all revved up, I wasn't down in the dumps either. It wasn't like those times when I just can't drag myself out of bed and everything feels like it's covered in wet cement, you know? I hate those days. When I get like that, I don't even care if they are messing with my numbers at the warehouse because I just can't bring myself to care about anything. But during that stretch I was just talking about? I wasn't depressed at all. I was just... level. 

I was getting up, having my coffee, making sure the kids had their lunches packed—which is a whole production in itself because my youngest won't eat anything with a crust, and my oldest is suddenly a vegetarian but only on Tuesdays, I swear, it's impossible to keep track of—but I was doing it. I was functioning totally fine. I didn't feel sad, I didn't feel hopeless, I wasn't crying for no reason. I was just going about my business, wrapping the pallets, checking the manifests. And the voice was just... there. It was like a coworker who just won't stop talking to you while you're trying to work. It wasn't making me sad, it was just making me aware of what the shift supervisor was trying to pull. So, no, I wouldn't say I was depressed at all when that was happening. Just normal, but, you know, dealing with the sabotage.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest in things most of the day nearly every day?

Two whole weeks? No, I don't think so. I mean, don't get me wrong, Dr. ____, I have days where I feel like absolute garbage, where I just want to pull the covers over my head and ignore the whole world. Especially after I've been running on empty for a while, you know, zooming around the warehouse and getting a million things done on zero sleep. Eventually, you just crash. Your body just gives out on you. But that’s only ever for a day, maybe two at the absolute most. I definitely haven't had it last for two whole weeks where I'm just depressed every single day. 

I literally don't have the time for that, to be honest. Between the freight schedules at work—which are always changing, by the way, they can never just give us a set roster—and trying to keep the house from falling apart, I can't just check out. If I don't go to work, we don't get paid, and my supervisor is already breathing down my neck about the pallet counts, so calling out sick for weeks because I'm feeling down just isn't an option in my world. Plus, the kids. I have to be there for them. Even if I'm feeling totally drained and just completely over it all, I still have to get up and make those lunches and do the laundry and make sure they get on the bus. 

So, no, it never stretches out that long. It's usually just a quick crash because I'm exhausted, and then I'm either back to regular, or my engine starts revving up again and I'm back to pacing the floors and doing a million things at once. But two straight weeks of just feeling hopeless and not caring about anything at all? No, I've never had that happen. I always bounce back way faster than that.
When you hear the voice, does it ever tell you to do things or comment on what you’re doing, or is it only warning you about the warehouse and your counts?

Well, it's... it's mostly about the checking, but it's not just like a vague warning, you know? It's really specific. Like, I'll be right in the middle of an aisle at the warehouse, pulling boxes for an order, totally focused on getting the labels right because they've been messing with the barcode scanner lately, I swear. And out of nowhere, clear as day, I'll hear this man's voice. It's not my supervisor's voice, it's deeper, but it sounds like someone is standing right next to my ear. And he'll say, "Nicole, check it again." 

And it's not just at work, either. That's the thing that really gets to me. I could be at home, standing in the laundry room, just folding clothes. Not thinking about work at all, just trying to match up my husband's socks, which is a nightmare because he buys these black ones that all look the same but have slightly different ribbing, and if I pair them wrong he complains. So I'm just standing there, minding my own business, folding the socks, and nobody is around. The kids are in the living room watching TV, my husband is out in the garage, I'm completely alone. And then I hear him again. "Nicole, check it again." 

And I'll spin around, thinking maybe my husband came inside and I didn't hear the door, or maybe the TV is too loud and I'm hearing a commercial or something. But there's nobody there. Just me and the laundry. And he just tells me to check things. Over and over. "Check it again." So I do. I check the socks, I check the washing machine dial, I check the dryer lint trap. Because if he's telling me to check it, there must be a reason, right? Just like at the warehouse. If he says to check the pallet, I check the pallet. He doesn't really tell me to do other things, like he doesn't tell me to make a sandwich or go to the store, he just constantly, constantly tells me to double-check whatever I'm doing. It's exhausting, honestly, because I'm already trying to keep track of so much, but when you hear someone right there, speaking directly to you, using your name... you listen, you know?
When you hear the voice, does it ever tell you to do things or comment on what you’re doing, or is it only warning you about the warehouse and your counts?

Like I was just trying to explain, it's really just focused on the checking. He doesn't sit there and narrate my whole day or tell me to do anything dangerous, thank God, because you hear about that kind of thing on those true crime shows and I absolutely could not handle that on top of everything else I have to deal with. But it is a direct command, you know? 

Sometimes when I'm in the aisle at work pulling stock, or, like I was just saying, folding clothes at home, I hear a man's voice clear as day saying, "Nicole, check it again." And it's so loud and so real that I'll literally drop whatever I'm holding. I'll peek around the pallet racks at the warehouse, thinking maybe one of the new guys is messing with me, because they do like to joke around on the floor and I really don't have the time or the patience for it. But I'll look, and the aisle will be completely empty. Or at home, I'll be totally alone in the laundry room, just me and a basket of shirts, not another person anywhere near me, and yet he's right there in my ear. 

"Nicole, check it again." 

He says it exactly like that, every single time, with this deep, serious tone. So it's not like we're having a conversation, and he's not commenting on my folding technique or anything like that, he's just strictly telling me to double-check my work, over and over, even when I am completely by myself and there is absolutely nobody near me who could have said it.
Have you had any times when you felt like your thoughts were being put into your head, taken out of your head, or broadcast so other people could hear them?

Put into my head? Like... like someone is beaming them in or something? No, no, definitely not. I mean, my head is always going a million miles a minute, don't get me wrong. Between keeping track of the inventory logs, remembering which pallets go to which loading dock—because I swear, if you put the outbound for Chicago on the dock for Detroit, the supervisor will absolutely lose his mind and it's always my fault somehow, even if the tags were printed wrong—and then trying to remember if I paid the electric bill or if I need to stop at the grocery store on the way home... my brain is just constantly full. It's packed. 

Honestly, sometimes I wish someone *would* take some thoughts out of my head just so I could get a break, you know? Just a few minutes of peace and quiet where I don't have to plan out the next five steps of my day. But no, they're all my thoughts. Nobody is putting them in there, except maybe my boss when he yells at me about the quotas, but that's just regular work stress, not like sci-fi mind control or whatever you're talking about. 

And people definitely can't hear what I'm thinking. Thank God for that, honestly. If the guys at the warehouse could hear what I was thinking about them when they leave their empty shrink-wrap rolls all over the aisle floor for me to trip over, I would have been fired years ago. I have some pretty choice words in my head sometimes when I'm pulling a double shift and my feet are just absolutely killing me and I just want to sit down for five seconds. If my thoughts were broadcasting like a radio station, I'd be in so much trouble. So, no. My thoughts stay right inside my own head. It's really crowded in there with everything I have to keep track of, but it's just me.
Have you ever had a period of at least a week when your mood was clearly elevated or euphoric, not just irritable, and other people noticed you were much more upbeat than usual?

Euphoric? I don't know if I'd use that exact word, that sounds like something you'd hear in a movie or something. But upbeat? Yeah, I guess. I mean, there are definitely times, like whole weeks sometimes, where I just wake up and I feel... well, I feel fired up. Like I have electricity running through me and absolutely nobody can slow me down. 

I'll go into the warehouse and I'm just tearing through the orders, moving faster than the guys who have been there forever. I feel invincible, honestly. Like I could work a double shift, reorganize the whole loading dock, and then go run a marathon. It feels amazing at first, it really does. I'm getting a million things done and my mind is just sharp, you know? 

But the problem is, it doesn't always stay happy or upbeat for very long. Because when I'm moving that fast and I'm feeling that good, I have zero patience for anyone interrupting my flow. Like, I'll get home, still riding that high, feeling like I can take on the world, and my husband will be sitting in the kitchen. And he'll ask just one small question. Something completely stupid and harmless, like asking about the kids' dentist appointments or what my schedule is for the rest of the week. 

And I just snap. I completely lose it on him. It's like, when I'm feeling that fired up and unstoppable, him asking about my schedule feels like he's trying to box me in or control me, you know? Like he's trying to put a leash on me and drag me down from this great place I'm in. So I'll just start yelling at him to back off and let me breathe and stop treating me like a child. So yeah, people definitely notice I'm acting different. They see me zooming around getting everything done, but they also learn pretty quick to stay out of my way, because the second they ask a simple question about the kids, I just bite their head off.
Have you ever had a period of at least one week when your mood was clearly elevated or irritable and you had much more energy than usual, even when you were not hearing voices or feeling paranoid?

No, see, it doesn't really work like that for me. It’s not like they take turns or anything. Like, I remember this one stretch... it went on for weeks, actually, where I was just completely wired. I was barely sleeping at all, maybe two hours a night if I was lucky, and I didn't even feel tired the next day. I was pushing all these extra shifts at the warehouse, just taking every single hour of overtime the supervisor would give me, and then I’d get off a ten- or twelve-hour shift and I still had so much electricity in my body I didn't know what to do with myself. 

So I started boxing. I found this gym near my house and I'd just go in there and hit the heavy bag for hours, just sweating it out, and then on top of that I was doing all this extra work at my church. I was organizing their whole donation pantry, sorting all the cans by expiration date, setting up the folding chairs for every single event they had... just going non-stop, a hundred miles an hour, from the second the sun came up until way past midnight. 

But even with all that energy, even when I was moving that fast, the other stuff didn't go away. During those exact same weeks, I was still hearing that man's voice. I'd be at the church sorting green beans and he'd be right there in my ear, telling me to check it again. And at the warehouse, while I was working all those extra shifts and moving faster than everybody else, I was absolutely sure that the other people on the floor were setting me up. I was looking over my shoulder constantly because I just knew they were messing with my pallets or hiding my scan gun to make me miss my quota so I'd get fired. I couldn't trust a single person in that building. 

So yeah, the high energy and the boxing and not sleeping... that was all happening at the exact same time I was hearing the voice and feeling completely paranoid about the guys at work. It doesn't give me a break. It all just piles on top of each other at the same time.
Have you ever had hallucinations or delusional beliefs for at least two weeks when you were not having any manic or depressed symptoms at all?

Yeah, actually... I mean, because you'd think if I just got some rest and slowed down, all of that would just go away, right? That's what my husband always says, he's always telling me I just need a good night's sleep. And there was this time, a while back, where I actually did get exactly that. It was a really quiet few weeks. I wasn't racing around as much, I wasn't taking all those crazy overtime shifts, and I definitely wasn't hitting the heavy bag at the gym until midnight. I was actually sleeping closer to normal. Like, going to bed at a decent hour, getting maybe six or seven hours of sleep, which is a total miracle for me. 

And my mood was completely fine during that stretch. I wasn't feeling all fired up with electricity, and I wasn't snapping at my husband over stupid questions. I was just... normal. Just a regular person going to work, doing my job, coming home, eating dinner, and going to bed. 

But the thing is, even during those quieter few weeks when my energy was totally leveled out and I was resting, the other stuff didn't stop. It didn't take a break just because my body did. I'd be at the warehouse, just working at a normal, steady pace, and I still heard that man's voice. Clear as day, right over the sound of the forklifts. He'd be right there in my ear, telling me to check things. "Check the tags again, check the shrink wrap, look behind the boxes, check it again." Just constantly telling me to check my work. 

And on top of that, I still absolutely believed that the pallet counts were being changed against me. I'd look at the loading manifest and the inventory screens, and I just knew—I knew for an absolute fact—that the other guys on the floor were going into the system and altering the numbers to screw up my quotas so I'd look bad to the supervisor. It didn't matter that I was sleeping fine and feeling completely calm, I still knew they were doing it. So, yeah... even when my mood is totally fine for weeks at a time, that voice telling me to check things and that whole situation with the pallet counts, it's still right there with me.
Have you ever had one continuous period of these hallucinations and paranoid beliefs that lasted a full month or longer?

A month? Oh, I wish it was just a month. It’s... well, let me think about it. It’s been way, way longer than that. I’d say the voices, and that whole feeling that people at the warehouse are watching me or changing my numbers around... that’s been happening for about eight months now. 

Yeah, eight whole months of this, straight through. It hasn't stopped once. Do you have any idea how exhausting that is? Waking up every single day for eight months straight and the very first thing I hear, before I even get my steel-toes laced up for work, is that man's voice telling me to check things. And then I get to the warehouse, and for eight months I've had this... this heavy, tight feeling right in the middle of my chest, just knowing that people are watching every move I make on the floor, knowing they are going into the system and changing my pallet counts just to screw with me. 

It's like a full-time job just trying to keep track of who is messing with my stuff, on top of my actual full-time job of moving the freight. And my husband, he just doesn't get it. He thinks I can just ignore it or turn it off, like it's a radio or something. But how do you turn it off when it's been going on every single day for almost three-quarters of a year? I mean, I've tried everything. I try putting in those little foam earplugs they give us for the forklift noise, I try just keeping my head down, but that man is still right there in my ear, "check the tags, check the wrap," over and over. And I'm still looking over my shoulder at the other guys on the floor, because I know what they're doing. Eight months of that... it wears you down to the bone, it really does. I used to be able to just go in, do my shift, and come home, but now... I mean, eight months is a really long time to feel like the whole building is out to get you, you know?
Has there been any point when the voices and paranoid beliefs stopped completely for at least a few days?

No... no, not at all. I mean, you'd think maybe if I wasn't at the warehouse, right? Like if I just had a couple days away from the floor, it would give it a rest. But it doesn't. Not even for a weekend. 

I remember when we had that long weekend for the holidays, the warehouse was completely shut down for three whole days. No freight moving, no forklifts, nothing. And I thought, okay, this is it, I'm just gonna sit on my couch and watch TV and finally get some peace and quiet in my own head. But I was sitting right there in my living room, trying to watch a movie with my husband, and that man's voice was right there with me. Clear as a bell. "Check the tags, check it again." I'm looking at my coffee table and he's telling me to check the shrink wrap. 

And even though the building was locked up tight, I was still sitting there just obsessing over the inventory screens in my head, just absolutely convinced that those guys were somehow logging into the system from home, you know? Like they were using the holiday weekend to mess with my pallet counts while I couldn't be there to defend myself. My husband was getting so frustrated with me because I couldn't even focus on the movie, I was just pacing around the kitchen. He kept asking me to just sit down and relax, but how do you relax when you haven't had a single day of peace in eight months? 

Not one day. Not a Saturday, not a Sunday. I wake up on my days off and it's just... it's already there waiting for me. There's no pause button on any of it. I've tried everything to just get a couple days of quiet. I've tried taking these really long, hot showers, I've tried sitting in the dark in the bedroom, I even tried driving out to the state park just to look at the trees and get away from the city, but it doesn't matter where I go. He just comes right along with me. The voice, the heavy feeling in my chest that I'm being set up at work... it's like a shadow. You can't outrun your own shadow, right? It's attached to you. So no, not even for a couple of days. It just never, ever stops.

Have the voice and suspicious beliefs been present only during times when you were having clear manic symptoms, or have they also been there during long stretches when your mood and energy were completely normal?

Well, like I think I was saying earlier... it really doesn't make a difference what my mood is doing. It’s there for both. It’s like it doesn't care if my engine is running hot or if I'm just coasting, you know? 

Because, sure, when I get into one of those phases where I'm just buzzing, like I've got electricity in my veins and I'm taking all those crazy overtime shifts and I feel like I don't even need to sleep... yeah, the voice is definitely there. He's telling me to check the tags, check the wrap, and I know for a fact the guys are messing with my pallet counts. That's usually when I end up getting into it with my husband the most, because I'm just so wound up and he doesn't understand why I'm pacing the kitchen floor at 2 AM talking about the loading manifest. 

But then... well, like I told you about that quiet stretch I had, where my energy was totally normal and I was actually getting my six or seven hours of sleep? The stuff didn't go away. I wasn't feeling hyper, I wasn't snapping at anybody, I was just having completely average days. Just a regular person going in, moving the freight, coming home, eating dinner, and watching TV. And even during those long stretches of just being totally fine and calm, I'm still hearing him. I'm still looking over my shoulder at the inventory screens. 

My husband actually tried keeping a little calendar on the fridge for a while, trying to see if my moods matched up with when I was complaining about the guys at work or the voice. He thought he was being a detective or something, trying to prove a point that it was just me being overtired or too wired up. But he gave up on it after a couple of months because there was just no pattern for him to find. Whether I'm bouncing off the concrete floors at the warehouse with all this crazy energy, or if I'm just sitting quietly on my couch feeling completely leveled out... it doesn't matter. The man's voice is right there in my ear, and those guys are still out to ruin my quotas. So yeah, it's absolutely there during the normal stretches, just as much as the other times.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest in things most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? No... no, I don't think so. I mean, you'd think I would be, right? With everything going on at the warehouse and never getting a moment of peace, you'd think I'd just want to give up. But I don't get like that. I've never had a stretch where I just felt sad or didn't care about things for weeks at a time. 

Even when it's really, really exhausting, I still care. I still want to go in and do my job, I still want to come home and watch my movies, I still want to eat a good dinner. My sister-in-law, now she gets depressed. She'll lay in the dark for days and not even take a shower, just completely checks out of her own life. But me? No, I don't sink down into some dark hole like that. Like I was saying before, sometimes my engine is running so hot I can't even stop moving, and other times I'm just coasting along on a regular day, but I never just drop down to zero. 

My husband, he sometimes asks me, "Are you sad? You look sad," especially when I'm just sitting there staring at the kitchen table. But I always have to tell him, "I'm not sad, I'm just busy." Because I'm not depressed, I'm just listening to that man's voice, or I'm trying to run the math in my head to figure out how the guys on the floor changed my pallet counts that shift.
